When Lawsuits Reveal Hidden Risks, Civil Justice, Children and Corporate Accountability

CEO Weekly Contributor

  • October 8, 2026
  • BRANDED CONTENT
  • Business
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:56
Instaread

A lawsuit can do more than resolve a dispute between two parties. In cases involving children and potentially harmful products, it can bring hidden information into public view, test corporate decisions against legal duties, and influence how industries respond to risk. As technology continues to develop faster than legislation, this role of civil litigation is becoming increasingly important.

The connection is especially clear in the growing debate over children and technology. On August 5, 2026, the Senate Commerce Committee advanced bipartisan measures addressing addictive technology design, artificial intelligence chatbots, children’s privacy, and parental controls. Later that month, Meta reached a multistate settlement resolving claims related to the design and safety of Facebook and Instagram for young users. Together, these developments show how legislation, enforcement and litigation can converge around emerging risks.

The Senate action included the Kids Online Safety Act, Youth AI Privacy Act, CHATBOT Act, and Children’s Artificial Intelligence Toy Safety Act. The measures address different concerns, including parental oversight, privacy, chatbot use, and safeguards for AI-enabled toys.

The committee’s action illustrates how lawmakers are attempting to address risks created by technologies that can reach children before long-standing regulatory frameworks have fully developed. The August 26 Meta settlement likewise required changes to access, time limits, age assurance, and protections for young users, while resolving state allegations. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

For attorney Paul Levin, the value of civil litigation lies partly in its ability to uncover information that families, journalists and even lawmakers may not otherwise obtain. Through discovery, legitimate lawsuits can bring internal research, safety analyses, testing data, corporate communications and other evidence before a court. That evidence can help determine what a company knew, what decisions were made, and whether those decisions contributed to an injury.

Levin has experienced this process through his work in mass tort litigation involving particularly vulnerable children. As a founding member of Levin, Rojas, Camassar & Reck, LLC, he helped initiate litigation concerning cow’s milk-based nutritional products provided to premature infants and claims involving necrotizing enterocolitis, commonly known as NEC. The firm filed its first case in 2019, and the litigation later became part of federal multidistrict litigation in the Northern District of Illinois.

Across these matters, Levin’s work reflects several related objectives: obtaining meaningful compensation for injured people, bringing preventable risks to public attention, and encouraging safer clinical and corporate practices. He is also a founder and managing member of the Connecticut Injury Firm, LLC, which handles serious and catastrophic injury matters involving medical malpractice, nursing home injuries, product liability, trucking accidents, and wrongful death.

The same principle can apply to technology. Social media platforms and artificial intelligence systems contain design choices that can affect young users, from recommendation systems and notifications to personalization, persistent memory, and conversational reinforcement. Levin argues that accountability should examine these choices rather than focusing only on what companies say about their products.

Levin has also begun bringing these issues to a wider audience through podcast appearances, articles, and other public forums addressing product safety, legal accountability, and the role of civil justice. He is also expanding his public commentary through articles and other forums where questions surrounding safety, accountability, and civil justice can be examined.

For Levin, regulation and litigation serve different purposes. Legislatures can establish broad standards, regulators can enforce them, and courts can examine specific claims through evidence. Preserving access to the courts therefore remains important as lawmakers address rapidly changing technologies and other products affecting children. Sometimes, the lawsuit does not simply respond to a known problem. It helps reveal why the problem required attention in the first place.
